slides.title: Mutex Locks
slides.body: Mutex Locks

slides.title: Mutex Locks - The Simplest Synchronization Tool
slides.body:
Peterson's Solution and hardware instructions work, but they are low-level and error-prone for application programmers. Operating systems provide a simpler abstraction: the mutex lock (mutual exclusion lock)
A Lock With Exactly Two States
slides.notes: While solutions like Peterson's algorithm and hardware instructions solve the problem, they are difficult for application programmers to work with. To simplify this, operating systems provide a higher-level abstraction called a mutex lock, also known as a mutual exclusion lock.

slides.title: Mutex Locks - The Simplest Synchronization Tool
slides.body:
A Lock With Exactly Two States
Mutex Lock: A Boolean-style synchronization tool with only two states, locked (unavailable) and unlocked (available)
Purpose: Protect a critical section so that only one process/thread can execute it at a time
Two Operations: Acquire() and release(), both must be atomic
slides.notes: ow, a mutex lock is a simple synchronization tool that works like a Boolean value, with just two states—locked, meaning it's unavailable, and unlocked, meaning it's available. Its purpose is to protect the critical section, allowing only one process or thread to execute it at a time. To achieve this, a mutex lock provides two atomic operations: acquire() to obtain the lock and release() to free it.

slides.title: Mutex Locks - The Simplest Synchronization Tool
slides.notes:
The acquire() function first checks whether the lock is already in use.
 If it is, the process keeps waiting in the while loop, a technique called spinning. 
Once the lock becomes free, locked = true acquires it atomically.
 After the critical section is complete, the release() function sets locked = false, 
making the lock available for the next process.

slides.title: Mutex Locks - The Simplest Synchronization Tool
slides.body:
acquire(lock)        // enter: take the lock
    // critical section
release(lock)        // exit: free the lock
Pseudocode
Ownership: the process that calls acquire() is the only one allowed to call release() on that lock, this is enforced by convention/runtime, unlike a semaphore
Usage Pattern
slides.notes: Moving on, the flow of using a mutex lock is quite simple. We begin by calling acquire() to secure the lock before executing the protected code. After the required operation is completed, release() is used to make the lock available again. Also, remember that the process which acquires the lock is the one expected to release it, which is a key difference from a semaphore.

slides.title: Mutex Locks - The Simplest Synchronization Tool
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: A mutex is like a single key hung outside a shared office cabin. Whoever takes the key can enter and work; everyone else waits outside. Only the person who took the key can hang it back — a stranger cannot walk up and return a key they never took.

slides.title: Mutex Locks in Practice
slides.body:
Advantages
Extremely simple API - just acquire() and release()
Ownership model prevents accidental release by the wrong process
Directly supported by hardware instructions (Test-and-Set / Compare-and-Swap) for atomicity
1
2
3
slides.notes: Next, let's look at why mutex locks are widely used in practice. They provide a simple interface, as synchronization is handled using just acquire() and release(). Another advantage is the ownership model, which ensures the lock is released only by the process that acquired it. Additionally, mutex locks rely on hardware-supported atomic instructions, making these operations safe and reliable.

slides.title: Mutex Locks in Practice
slides.body:
The naive version above uses busy waiting — the CPU is wasted while a process spins
Can only guard one resource at a time (binary) — cannot represent a pool of N identical resources the way a counting semaphore can
Mutexes are meant for mutual exclusion only; they are not designed for signalling between processes ("wake someone else up when an event happens") the way semaphores are
1
2
3
Limitations
slides.notes: The basic implementation relies on busy waiting, where a process keeps checking for the lock instead of doing useful work, leading to CPU wastage. Also, a mutex can protect only one resource at a time, unlike a counting semaphore. Finally, mutexes are designed purely for mutual exclusion and not for signalling or notifying other processes when an event occurs.

slides.title: Semaphores
slides.body: Semaphores
slides.notes: Next we will be learning about the Semaphores

slides.title: Introduction to Semaphores
slides.body:
What is a Semaphore?
A semaphore is a synchronization primitive used to control access to a shared resource by multiple processes or threads
What is a Semaphore?
 It helps prevent race conditions and ensures proper coordination between processes
slides.notes: Now, let's move on to another important synchronization mechanism called a semaphore. Unlike a mutex, a semaphore is used to coordinate how multiple processes or threads access a shared resource. By regulating this access, it helps avoid race conditions and ensures that processes work together in a synchronized manner.

slides.title: Introduction to Semaphores
slides.body:
Key Characteristics
It is an integer variable whose value is modified only through two atomic operations: wait() and signal()
Can be used to allow one or multiple processes into the critical section
slides.notes: Next, let's look at the key characteristics of a semaphore. A semaphore is maintained as an integer variable, and its value can be changed only through the atomic operations wait() and signal(). Depending on its type, it can either allow only one process to access the critical section or multiple processes to access it simultaneously.

slides.title: Introduction to Semaphores
slides.body:
Key Characteristics
Ensures synchronization without race conditions
Simple but powerful mechanism widely used in OS
slides.notes: Continuing with the Characteristics , semaphores play an important role in keeping concurrent execution safe by ensuring that processes are synchronized and race conditions are avoided. Despite having a simple working mechanism, they are versatile enough to handle different synchronization scenarios, which is why they are widely used in operating systems.

slides.title: Introduction to Semaphores
slides.body:
Two Atomic Operations
wait() (P / down / acquire)
wait(S) {
    while (S <= 0) { }   // busy wait: spin until a unit is free
    S--                  // take one unit (check + decrement must be atomic)
}
Pseudocode
Decrements the semaphore value
If S ≤ 0 → process must wait
P stands for Proberen (to test)
In modern OS, processes do NOT busy-wait; they are blocked and put into a waiting queue
slides.notes: Now let's look at the wait() operation. It first checks whether the semaphore S is available. If S ≤ 0, the process must wait. Otherwise, S-- decrements the semaphore value atomically, reserving one unit of the resource. This operation is also called P (Proberen), down, or acquire. Although the pseudocode shows busy waiting, modern operating systems block the process and  it in a waiting queue until the resource becomes available.

slides.title: Introduction to Semaphores
slides.body:
Two Atomic Operations
signal() (V / up / release)
signal(S) {
    S++      // release one unit (must be atomic)
}
Syntax
Increments semaphore value
Wakes up a blocked process (if any)
V stands for Verhogen (to increment)
slides.notes: Now let's understand the signal() operation. It performs the opposite task of wait(). The statement S++ increments the semaphore value atomically, indicating that one unit of the resource has been released. If any process is waiting, the signal() operation wakes up one blocked process. This operation is also known as V (Verhogen), up, or release.

slides.title: Introduction to Semaphores
slides.body:
Why Atomic ?
Two processes must never execute wait() or signal() on the same semaphore at the same time
Prevents race conditions
Guaranteed by hardware (atomic instructions) or OS kernel
slides.notes: Moving on, both wait() and signal() must execute atomically, meaning one process should complete the operation before another can access the same semaphore. This prevents multiple processes from modifying the semaphore simultaneously, thereby avoiding race conditions. Such atomic execution is typically ensured by hardware-supported atomic instructions or by the operating system kernel.

slides.title: Introduction to Semaphores
slides.body:
Types of Semaphores
Counting Semaphore
Binary Semaphore
Semaphores are mainly of two Types
slides.notes: Now, based on how they are used, semaphores are broadly classified into two types: Counting Semaphores and Binary Semaphores.

slides.title: Types of Semaphores
slides.body:
Binary Semaphore
Critical section
Binary semaphore
0
1
Or
A semaphore that can take only two values: 0 and 1
Controls mutual exclusion for a single resource or critical section
1 → process can enter CS, 0 → process must wait
slides.notes:
Next, let's begin with the Binary Semaphore. As the name suggests, it can hold only two values—0 and 1. 
Because of this, it is used to control access to a single resource or critical section. When the semaphore value is 1, a process is allowed to proceed. If the value becomes 0, any other process requesting access has to wait until it becomes available again.

slides.title: Binary Semaphore
slides.body:
Operation
Example: Single printer
wait() → decrements value, process enters CS
signal() → increments value, resource released
slides.notes: let's see how a Binary Semaphore operates. A process calls wait() before accessing the resource, which decreases the semaphore value and allows it to enter the critical section. Once the task is completed, it invokes signal() to increase the value, indicating that the resource is available again. A common example is managing access to a single printer, where only one process can use it at a time.

slides.title: Binary Semaphore
slides.notes: A Binary Semaphore can have only two values, 0 or 1, making it useful for mutual exclusion. In this example, S is initialized to 1, so P1 executes wait(S), changes it to 0, and enters the critical section. When P2 calls wait(S), it finds S = 0 and gets blocked. Once P1 finishes, it executes signal(S), changing S back to 1 and allowing P2 to proceed. This is why a binary semaphore is commonly used as a mutex to ensure only one process accesses the critical section at a time.

slides.title: Types of Semaphores
slides.body:
Counting Semaphore
A semaphore whose value can range from 0 to N
Controls access to multiple instances of a resource
Semaphore value = number of available resources
If value > 0 → processes can access resources
If value = 0 → processes must wait
Counting Semaphore
slides.notes: Next, let's look at the Counting Semaphore. Unlike a binary semaphore, its value can range from 0 to N, making it suitable for managing multiple instances of the same resource. The semaphore value represents the number of resources currently available. As long as the value is greater than zero, processes can continue accessing the resources. Once it reaches zero, any additional process has to wait until a resource becomes available again.

slides.title: Counting Semaphore
slides.body:
Example
Example: 3 printers, multiple processes can print simultaneously
Process 1
Process 2
Process 3
slides.notes: Moving on, let's understand this with a simple example. Suppose a system has three printers available. Since multiple instances of the resource exist, a counting semaphore is a suitable choice. This allows up to three processes to use the printers at the same time, as illustrated by the processes shown here.

slides.title: Counting Semaphore
slides.notes: Here, S is initialized to n, indicating that n resources are available. Each wait(S) decrements the semaphore and allocates one resource, while signal(S) increments it when the resource is released. For example, if there are 3 printers, wait(printers) reduces the count to 2 when one printer is in use, and signal(printers) restores it to 3 after the printer is released.

slides.title: Introduction to Semaphores
slides.body:
Advantages
Simplicity
Easy to understand and implement
Only two operations: wait() and signal()
No Busy Waiting
Processes sleep when waiting instead of spinning
Improves CPU utilization
slides.notes: Next, let's look at some advantages of semaphores. One of the biggest benefits is their simplicity, as synchronization is handled using just two operations—wait() and signal(). Another advantage is that, in modern operating systems, a process waiting for a resource is put to sleep instead of continuously checking for it, which avoids busy waiting and leads to better CPU utilization.

slides.title: Introduction to Semaphores
slides.body:
Advantages
Versatility
Can solve mutual exclusion and synchronization ordering problems
Works for single or multiple resource control
Portability
Supported by most operating systems
Standard synchronization primitive
slides.notes: semaphores are also valued for their versatility. They can be used not only to provide mutual exclusion but also to maintain the required execution order between processes. Depending on the requirement, they can manage either a single resource or multiple resources. Another advantage is their portability, as semaphores are supported by most operating systems and are a widely adopted synchronization mechanism.

slides.title: Introduction to Semaphores
slides.body:
Advantages
Efficiency
Low overhead with proper OS/hardware implementation
Faster than purely software-based solutions
slides.notes: Finally, semaphores are also efficient. With support from the operating system and hardware, they perform synchronization with low overhead, making them faster than solutions implemented purely in software.

slides.title: Introduction to Semaphores
slides.body:
Disadvantages
Programming Errors
Mistakes in wait()/signal() ordering can cause deadlocks
Hard to debug in complex programs
No Ownership
Any process can call signal()
Unlike mutex, this can lead to logical errors
slides.notes: Moving on, semaphores also have some limitations. If wait() and signal() are not placed correctly in a program, processes may end up waiting indefinitely, and identifying such issues can become difficult as the program grows larger. Also, unlike a mutex, a semaphore does not track which process should release it, so incorrect use can introduce unexpected synchronization problems.

slides.title: Introduction to Semaphores
slides.body:
Disadvantages
Priority Inversion
A low-priority process holding a semaphore can block high-priority processes
May cause unpredictable delays
    Risk of Processes Blocking Forever
Incorrect ordering of wait()/signal() can cause processes to block each other permanently, so none can continue.
slides.notes: Moving on , semaphores can also introduce priority inversion, where a high-priority process is forced to wait because the required semaphore is held by a lower-priority process, leading to unexpected delays. Another risk is that if wait() and signal() are not coordinated correctly, processes may end up waiting on one another indefinitely, preventing any of them from making further progress.

slides.title: Introduction to Semaphores
slides.body:
Disadvantages
Limited Error Detection
OS does not detect improper usage automatically
Programmer must ensure correct usage
slides.notes: Finally, semaphores provide very little built-in protection against incorrect usage. If they are used improperly, the operating system typically does not identify the mistake automatically. As a result, it is the programmer's responsibility to use semaphore operations correctly to ensure proper synchronization.

slides.title: Semaphore Implementation
slides.body: Semaphore Implementation
slides.notes: Next we will learn about the Semaphore Implementation

slides.title: Implementation Strategies
slides.notes: Next, let's look at the busy waiting implementation of a semaphore. In this approach, a process repeatedly checks whether the semaphore has become available instead of giving up the CPU. As shown in the pseudocode, wait(S) keeps looping until the semaphore can be acquired and then decrements its value atomically. Once the work is finished, signal(S) increments the semaphore value, making the resource available again.

slides.title: Implementation Strategies
slides.body:
The waiting process stays in the Running state, continuously consuming CPU cycles
Simple to implement, and there is no context-switch overhead
Wasteful and impractical if the wait is expected to be long — the CPU could be doing useful work for another process
Acceptable only when critical sections are extremely short (used inside multiprocessor kernels for short locks)
1. Busy Waiting Implementation
slides.notes: Moving on, in a busy waiting implementation, a waiting process continues to run while repeatedly checking the semaphore, which keeps the CPU occupied. Although this approach is simple and avoids the overhead of context switching, it becomes inefficient when the waiting time is long because CPU time is wasted. For this reason, it is generally suitable only for very short critical sections.

slides.title: Implementation Strategies
slides.body:
2. Block-and-Wakeup Implementation
The practical implementation used in real operating systems. The semaphore is defined as a structure, not a plain integer:
slides.notes: Next, let's look at the block-and-wakeup implementation, which is the approach used in real operating systems. Instead of treating a semaphore as just an integer, the operating system represents it as a data structure, allowing it to manage waiting processes more effectively.

slides.title: Implementation Strategies
slides.notes: This implementation avoids busy waiting. The Semaphore structure stores the current semaphore value and a queue of blocked processes. In wait(S), the semaphore value is first decremented. If the value becomes less than 0, it means no resource is available, so the current process is added to the waiting queue and block() moves it to the Waiting state, freeing the CPU for other processes.

slides.title: Implementation Strategies
slides.notes: The signal(S) operation releases a resource by incrementing the semaphore value. If the updated value is less than or equal to 0, it means there are processes waiting in the queue. One process is removed from the queue, and wakeup(P) moves it from the Waiting state to the Ready state so it can resume execution when the CPU is available.

slides.title: Implementation Strategies
slides.body:
block() suspends the calling process, moving it from Running to the Waiting state and placing it on the semaphore's own waiting list
wakeup(P) moves a specific process P from Waiting to Ready, so the scheduler can run it again
No CPU cycles wasted while a process waits, it simply is not scheduled until woken
This is the implementation used by real OS kernels (Linux, Windows) for general-purpose semaphores
2. Block-and-Wakeup Implementation
slides.notes: in the block-and-wakeup implementation, a process that cannot proceed calls block(), which suspends it and places it in the semaphore's waiting list. When the resource becomes available, wakeup(P) moves the waiting process back to the Ready state so it can be scheduled again. Since waiting processes are not repeatedly checking the semaphore, no CPU time is wasted, making this the approach used by modern operating systems such as Linux and Windows.

slides.title: Implementation Strategies
slides.body: Comparison
tables: Very short critical sections, multiprocessor spinlocks

slides.title: Busy Waiting
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Busy waiting is like standing at a locked door, repeatedly rattling the handle every second until it opens — you get nothing else done.

slides.title: Block-and-Wakeup
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes:
Block-and-wakeup is like leaving your name with the receptionist 
and going to sit down; you are called back only when the door actually opens.

slides.title: Monitors & Critical Regions
slides.body: Monitors & Critical Regions
slides.notes: Next we will learn about the Monitors and Critical Regions

slides.title: Monitors & Critical Regions
slides.body:
A monitor is a higher-level, language-supported construct that removes this burden from the programmer
What is Monitor?
Semaphores work, but every wait()/signal() pairing is manual, a single missed call anywhere in the program breaks the whole system.
slides.notes: Although semaphores are effective, they require programmers to manually coordinate every wait() and signal() call. Missing even a single operation can lead to synchronization problems.A monitor addresses this by providing a higher-level, language-supported mechanism that simplifies synchronization and reduces the chances of such programming mistakes.

slides.title: High-Level Synchronization Mechanism
slides.body:
Monitor: An Abstract Data Type (ADT) that bundles together shared data, the procedures that operate on that data, and initialization code, all inside one construct
Automatic mutual exclusion: A monitor guarantees that only one process can execute inside it at a time. The compiler/runtime automatically handles locking, so programmers don't need explicit lock/unlock operations to enter or leave the monitor
Monitors
slides.notes: Moving on, a Monitor is a high-level synchronization construct implemented as an Abstract Data Type (ADT). It keeps the shared data, the operations performed on that data, and the required initialization together in one place, making synchronization easier to organize. Another important feature is automatic mutual exclusion. Instead of writing explicit lock and unlock operations, the language or runtime ensures that only one process can execute inside the monitor at a time.

slides.title: Monitors - Synchronization Built Into the Language
slides.notes: he statement monitor MonitorName defines a monitor that contains the shared data and the procedures operating on it. Inside the monitor, P1() and P2() are procedures that access the shared variables. The important rule is that only one process or thread can execute any monitor procedure at a time, ensuring safe access to the shared data automatically.

slides.title: Monitors - Synchronization Built Into the Language
slides.body:
Key Characteristics
Any process calling one of the monitor's procedures automatically waits (outside) if another process is already executing inside the monitor
This guarantees mutual exclusion on the shared data without a single explicit lock call in the calling code
Monitors are a language-level construct, supported in Java (synchronized keyword + Object.wait/notify), C#, and taught conceptually in Concurrent Pascal, the language that introduced them
slides.notes: Next, let's look at the key characteristics of monitors. Whenever a process invokes a monitor procedure, it can enter only if no other process is currently executing inside the monitor. This built-in behavior ensures mutual exclusion without requiring explicit lock operations in the calling code. Since monitors are a language-level construct, they are directly supported in languages such as Java and C#, and were originally introduced through Concurrent Pascal.

slides.title: Monitors - Synchronization Built Into the Language
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: A monitor is like a principal's office that allows only one student inside at a time. If another student arrives while someone is already inside, they automatically wait outside. The students don't lock or unlock the door themselves—the office rules enforce one-at-a-time access.

slides.title: Waiting on a Condition - Not Just a Lock
slides.body:
Mutual exclusion alone is not enough, a process inside the monitor may need to pause until some internal condition becomes true (e.g., "wait until the buffer is not full"). Monitors provide condition variables for exactly this
Condition Variables
slides.notes: Next, mutual exclusion by itself cannot solve every synchronization problem. Sometimes, a process is allowed to enter the monitor but still cannot continue because a required condition has not yet been satisfied—for example, waiting until a buffer has free space. To handle such situations, monitors provide condition variables, allowing a process to wait until the required condition becomes true.

slides.title: Waiting on a Condition - Not Just a Lock
slides.notes: Condition variables are used inside a monitor to allow processes to wait for a specific condition. Here, condition x, y declares two condition variables. When a process calls x.wait(), it releases the monitor and moves to the waiting state until the condition is satisfied. Later, another process calls x.signal(), which wakes up one waiting process, if any, allowing it to continue execution.

slides.title: Condition Variables
slides.body:
x.wait(): The calling process suspends itself on condition x and steps outside the monitor's mutual-exclusion boundary, allowing another process to enter
x.signal(): Resumes exactly one process suspended on x, if any exist. If no process is waiting on x, the signal has no effect and is simply lost 
x.wait() and x.signal()
slides.notes: Next, let's understand the two operations provided by condition variables. When a process calls x.wait(), it temporarily suspends its execution and leaves the monitor, allowing another process to enter and continue working. Later, when the required condition is satisfied, another process can call x.signal() to wake one waiting process. If no process is waiting on that condition, the signal is simply ignored.

slides.title: Waiting on a Condition - Not Just a Lock
slides.body:
Hoare monitors (signal-and-wait)
The signalling process immediately pauses, and the newly-woken process runs immediately with a guarantee that the condition it waited for is still true.
Mesa monitors (signal-and-continue)
The signalling process keeps running, and the awakened process becomes Ready until it re-enters the monitor. It must recheck the condition with while, as the condition may have changed meanwhile
Two well-known semantics for what happens right after x.signal():
Hoare Monitors & Mesa Monitors
slides.notes: Next, the behavior of a monitor after x.signal() depends on the synchronization semantics it follows. In Hoare monitors, control is handed over immediately to the waiting process, while the signalling process waits until that process finishes or leaves the monitor. In Mesa monitors, the signalling process continues its execution first, and the awakened process simply moves to the Ready state. When it later gets another chance to enter the monitor, it must recheck the condition using a while loop, because the condition it was waiting for might no longer be true.

slides.title: Semaphore & Monitor Condition Variable
slides.body: Comparison

slides.title: A Language Construct for Guarded Shared Access
slides.body:
Before monitors, C.A.R. Hoare and Per Brinch Hansen proposed the conditional critical region, a language construct that ties a shared variable directly to the code blocks allowed to touch it
Conditional Critical Regions
Shared variable declaration: a variable is explicitly declared as shared, so the compiler knows it needs protection
slides.notes: Next, before monitors were introduced, C.A.R. Hoare and Per Brinch Hansen proposed Conditional Critical Regions as a language-level approach for synchronization. The main idea was to associate a shared variable directly with the code that is permitted to access it. By explicitly declaring a variable as shared, the compiler recognizes that it requires controlled and protected access whenever multiple processes may use it concurrently.

slides.title: Conditional Critical Regions
slides.body:
Example
var v : shared T;        // v is a shared, protected variable
region v when (B) do     // enter only when condition B is true
    S;                   // execute guarded statements S
                         // if B is false, wait (no busy-waiting)
Pseudocode
slides.notes: Conditional Critical Regions provide synchronized access based on a condition. Here, v is the shared protected variable, and B is a Boolean condition that determines whether a process can enter the critical region. The statement region v when (B) do allows the process to execute the guarded statements S only if B is true. If the condition is false, the process waits without busy waiting until it becomes true.

slides.title: Conditional Critical Regions - A Precursor to Monitors
slides.body:
Region v when B do S, a process may enter the critical region on shared variable v only when boolean condition B is true; it then executes statement block S
If B is false, the process waits (without busy-waiting) until some other process's action makes B true
Key Behaviors
slides.notes: Moving on, Conditional Critical Regions use the construct region v when B do S to control access to shared data. Here, v represents the shared variable, B is the Boolean condition that must be satisfied, and S is the statement block to be executed. A process can enter the region only when B is true. Otherwise, it waits without busy-waiting until another process changes the shared state, making the condition true.

slides.title: Conditional Critical Regions - A Precursor to Monitors
slides.body:
Key Behaviors
What it does:
The region v when (B) construct allows execution only when condition B is true, providing mutual exclusion and conditional synchronization in a single step
Why it helps:
It provides structured, language-level synchronization by restricting shared data access to a defined region, making correct use natural and reducing errors compared to manual wait()/signal() synchronization
slides.notes: Next, the region v when (B) construct combines mutual exclusion and conditional synchronization into a single language statement. A process can execute the associated code only when the condition B is satisfied, ensuring that shared data is accessed safely. Since this synchronization is built into the language, programmers don't have to manually coordinate wait() and signal() operations, making concurrent programs easier to write and less prone to synchronization errors.

slides.title: Conditional Critical Regions - A Precursor to Monitors
slides.body:
Key Behaviors
Relationship to monitors
Critical regions and monitors solve the same problem (structured synchronization), but monitors also bundle shared data and its operations into a single module, which is why monitors were more widely adopted
slides.notes: Finally, Conditional Critical Regions and monitors are both designed to achieve structured synchronization, but they differ in how they organize shared resources. While Conditional Critical Regions focus on controlling access to a shared variable, monitors go a step further by grouping the shared data and the operations performed on it into a single module. This integrated design makes monitors easier to use and is one of the main reasons they became the more widely adopted synchronization mechanism.

slides.title: Conditional Critical Regions - A Precursor to Monitors
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: A critical region is like a locker that opens only when a condition light turns green. If the light is red (the condition is false),the process simply waits — and the locker's own mechanism checks the condition and lets the process in automatically the moment it turns green, with no manual checking or busy-waiting.
